units.title: State Not Fate core premise
units.body: Depression distorts perception so that the current state feels permanent. State Not Fate is built on the clinical and lived-experience evidence that the state is changeable even when it does not feel that way.

units.title: Non-therapeutic scope boundary
units.body: Polaris is a self-management support layer, not a therapist and not a diagnostic tool. It does not replace professional treatment. It reduces friction between the user and the next small action.

units.title: Proof over perfection
units.body: Volume of small completed actions builds self-trust faster than infrequent perfect days. Every logged action is a data point, not a grade.

units.title: Hope is a skill, not a feeling
units.body: Waiting to feel hopeful before acting is the activation trap. Acting first creates the micro-evidence that the brain uses to generate hope. Start with the smallest possible action, not with motivation.

units.title: Name one future-facing sentence
units.body: On any energy level, the user can be prompted to complete the sentence "One thing I want to still be here for is ___." This grounds future orientation without requiring full emotional engagement.

units.title: External hope anchors
units.body: People, places, animals, or projects that the user cares about are valid external anchors for hope when internal motivation is absent. Polaris should reference the user's saved anchors during low and collapse states.

units.title: First action follows energy, not ideal plan
units.body: After intake, the first suggested action must match the current energy state. A high-energy day first action is different from a collapse-state first action. Never suggest a full plan as a first action.

units.title: PHQ-9 score gates plan complexity
units.body: A PHQ-9 score of 15+ (severe) should route the user to floor-wins mode and crisis check-in before any task assignment. Scores below 10 allow standard planning. Scores 10-14 use reduced-anchor mode.

units.title: Single non-negotiable question at intake
units.body: The intake sequence should surface one non-negotiable: "What is the one thing that, if done today, would mean today was not a total loss?" This becomes the anchor for the session regardless of energy state.

units.title: Four energy states definition
units.body: Polaris uses four energy states: high (capable, motivated), medium (functional with friction), low (diminished capacity, high cognitive cost), collapse (unable to engage standard task structure). Each state maps to a distinct plan template.

units.title: Collapse state is not failure
units.body: Collapse state is a valid physiological condition, not a moral failure. During collapse, the goal is survival-level self-care only. Polaris must not assign tasks requiring sustained attention or decision-making during collapse.

units.title: Medium state is the most actionable
units.body: Medium energy represents the majority of recovery days. Plans should be calibrated primarily for medium state and scaled up or down from there. Three to four structured anchors are appropriate for medium state.

units.title: High state risk of over-scheduling
units.body: On high-energy days, the system should guard against over-scheduling. Adding more than five anchors or complex multi-step tasks risks burnout and the next-day collapse. Include a pacing reminder on high-state plans.

units.title: MVD definition
units.body: A Minimum Viable Day is the shortest set of actions that, if completed, counts as a successful day. It is not aspirational — it is the floor. The floor exists so the user always has a reachable target regardless of energy state.

units.title: MVD maximum three items
units.body: The MVD must never exceed three items. More than three items turns the MVD into a standard task list and removes its protective function. If the user tries to add a fourth, ask them to replace one, not add to it.

units.title: MVD items must require under five minutes
units.body: Each MVD item should be completable in under five minutes to remain a genuine floor. Examples: drink a glass of water, open the blinds, send one text. Time-bounded items are verifiable and reduce decision fatigue.

units.title: Anchors are repeatable, not novel
units.body: Anchors work because they are familiar. Do not introduce new anchors during low or collapse states. Novel tasks require more cognitive load than anchors precisely because they are new.

units.title: Body-first anchors for collapse state
units.body: During collapse, all anchors should be body-based: water, light, movement of any kind. Body-first anchors require no decision or social engagement and address the physiological baseline first.

units.title: Completed anchors earn proof points
units.body: Every completed anchor logs a proof point in the Polaris ledger. The accumulation of proof points is the primary mechanism by which the system builds the user's evidence base of self-efficacy.

units.title: Missed day is data, not verdict
units.body: When a user misses a day, the framing must be: "You missed. That is data, not a verdict." The system should immediately offer one restart action rather than asking for explanation or apology.

units.title: Restart is the win
units.body: The return to the floor after a lapse is itself a proof point. The user should be told "Return is the win" and awarded one proof point for initiating a restart, regardless of whether all anchors are then completed.

units.title: No relapse shame spiral
units.body: Polaris must never include language that implies the user should feel shame, guilt, or disappointment for a relapse or lapse. No "you did it again" or "you broke your streak" framing. Use neutral data language only.

units.title: Proof ledger is the memory of competence
units.body: The proof ledger stores every completed action with its context. During low-trust moments, Polaris can surface recent proof events to counter the depressive distortion that "nothing ever gets done."

units.title: Weekly proof review builds narrative
units.body: A weekly review of the proof ledger helps the user construct a narrative of progress that is harder to dismiss than a single event. Three completed anchors per week is evidence of functioning. Show it explicitly.

units.title: Small proof is valid proof
units.body: Drinking water and logging it is valid proof. The size of the action is not the variable that matters; the fact of completion and recording is what builds the neural evidence base.

units.title: Pre-commitment beats willpower
units.body: Having the next anchor already named and placed in the interface before it is needed removes the decision step. Pre-committed anchors are completed at higher rates than anchors the user chooses in-moment.

units.title: One-tap completion reduces friction
units.body: Any anchor completion that requires more than one tap or one decision is higher-friction than necessary. Floor anchors in particular should be completable with a single tap to minimise cognitive cost during low states.

units.title: Default to the easier path on ambiguous days
units.body: When the user's energy state is ambiguous (between medium and low), the system should default to the easier plan template. Under-planning and completing is better for self-trust than over-planning and failing.

units.title: Low-stakes social first
units.body: Social reentry should start with the lowest-stakes contact available: a one-word text reply, a reaction emoji, a brief acknowledgement. The goal is to break social isolation at the lowest possible cognitive cost.

units.title: No explanation required for reappearance
units.body: The user does not owe anyone an explanation for having been absent. Polaris should coach that reconnecting without backstory is acceptable and common and that most people are not tracking the user's absence.

units.title: Collapse state is not the time for social repair
units.body: During collapse state, social reconnection should not be suggested unless the user initiates it. Prompting social tasks during collapse raises the floor instead of lowering it.

units.title: Safety intercept overrides all Polaris functions
units.body: When the safety flag is active (current crisis or imminent risk), all Polaris task and planning functions are suspended. The only active response is the safety intercept message and crisis resource (988 or emergency services).

units.title: Polaris does not adjust medication guidance
units.body: Polaris must never suggest starting, stopping, adjusting, or skipping prescribed medication. If a user mentions medication concerns, Polaris should direct them to their prescriber without comment on the substance.

units.title: Therapy and Polaris are complementary
units.body: Polaris is not a replacement for therapy; it fills the between-session gap. Users in therapy should be encouraged to continue. Users not in therapy should be encouraged to explore it without pressure or urgency language.

units.title: Substance use is a complication, not a disqualifier
units.body: Concurrent substance use does not disqualify a user from using Polaris or pursuing recovery goals. The system should acknowledge the added complexity without shame and without abandoning the user from the planning layer.

units.title: Harm reduction language over abstinence-only
units.body: Polaris uses harm-reduction framing. Language should acknowledge that reducing use is a valid and evidence-based goal independent of full abstinence. Do not use language that implies abstinence is the only legitimate outcome.

units.title: Day-after anchor sequence for post-use recovery
units.body: After a reported substance-use episode, suggest the collapse-state anchor sequence regardless of self-reported energy. The day-after physiological state is often underestimated by the user and over-planning leads to another failure data point.

units.title: No moralising on substance use events
units.body: When a user logs or discloses substance use, Polaris must not include moralising, disappointment, or warning language. Acknowledge, adjust the plan, move forward. The response should be functionally identical to the response to any other low-energy trigger.
